#hello-world-API-promts


#### Author
Santiago Hernandez
#### Prompt
<html>
  <head>

  </head>
  <body>
    <p style="margin-top: 0px">
      Does go not have a more explicit way to let a service only accept one 
      type of http request without having to add that validation code?
    </p>
  </body>
</html>


#### Answer **
<html>
  <head>

  </head>
  <body>
    <p style="margin-top: 0px">
      Yes &#8212; since <strong>Go 1.22</strong>, <code>net/http.ServeMux</code> 
      supports method-scoped patterns natively, so the manual guard is no 
      longer needed.
    </p>
    <h3>
      The built-in way
    </h3>
    <pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="150,220" data-copilot-content-offset="156,217" data-copilot-code-block-index="0" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>mux.HandleFunc(&quot;GET /api/v1/hello-world&quot;, helloWorldHandler)</code></pre>
    <p>
      Pattern syntax is <code>[METHOD ][HOST]/[PATH]</code>. The method is 
      separated from the path by a <strong>single space</strong>.
    </p>
    <p>
      What the mux does for you automatically:
    </p>
    <ul>
      <li>
        Routes only GET to that handler
      </li>
      <li>
        Returns <strong>405 Method Not Allowed</strong> for other verbs on 
        that same path
      </li>
      <li>
        Sets the <code>Allow</code> header listing the registered methods
      </li>
      <li>
        Matches <strong>HEAD</strong> whenever <code>GET</code> is registered
      </li>
      <li>
        Still returns <strong>404</strong> for paths that aren't registered at 
        all
      </li>
    </ul>
    <p>
      So your entire validation block collapses to nothing.
    </p>
    <h3>
      Applied to <code>server.go</code>
    </h3>
    <pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="726,1145" data-copilot-content-offset="732,1142" data-copilot-code-block-index="1" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>package main

import &quot;net/http&quot;

const helloWorldPath = &quot;/api/v1/hello-world&quot;

func newRouter() http.Handler {
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.HandleFunc(&quot;GET &quot;+helloWorldPath, helloWorldHandler)
return mux
}

func helloWorldHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
w.Header().Set(&quot;Content-Type&quot;, &quot;text/plain; charset=utf-8&quot;)
w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
_, _ = w.Write([]byte(&quot;Hello, World!&quot;))
}</code></pre>
<h3>
Other pattern features you get for free
</h3>
<pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="1191,1507" data-copilot-content-offset="1197,1504" data-copilot-code-block-index="2" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>mux.HandleFunc(&quot;GET /users/{id}&quot;, getUser)        // path wildcard
mux.HandleFunc(&quot;POST /users&quot;, createUser)         // different verb, same-ish path
mux.HandleFunc(&quot;GET /files/{path...}&quot;, serveFile) // multi-segment wildcard
mux.HandleFunc(&quot;GET /exact/{$}&quot;, exactOnly)       // anchors the end of the path</code></pre>
<p>
Read a wildcard inside the handler with:
</p>
<pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="1550,1583" data-copilot-content-offset="1556,1580" data-copilot-code-block-index="3" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>id := r.PathValue(&quot;id&quot;)</code></pre>
<h3>
Caveats
</h3>
<ul>
<li>
<strong>Go version matters.</strong> Patterns are opt-in via the <code>go</code>
directive in <code>go.mod</code>. Yours says <code>go 1.27</code>, so
you're fine. A module declaring <code>go 1.21</code> or lower keeps
the old literal-path behavior and would treat <code>&quot;GET /foo&quot;</code>
as a path containing a space.
</li>
<li>
<strong>Method names are case-sensitive</strong> and must be
uppercase: <code>GET</code>, not <code>get</code>.
</li>
<li>
<strong>Registering the same method+path twice panics</strong> at
startup.
</li>
<li>
<code>HEAD</code> is auto-handled for <code>GET</code> routes, but if
you register <code>HEAD</code> explicitly it takes precedence.
</li>
</ul>
<h3>
Before Go 1.22
</h3>
<p>
The old options were exactly what you'd expect:
</p>
<ol>
<li>
Manual <code>if r.Method != ...</code> checks (what you had)
</li>
<li>
A middleware wrapper, e.g. <code>allowMethod(&quot;GET&quot;, handler)</code>
</li>
<li>
A third-party router &#8212; <code>chi</code>, <code>gorilla/mux</code>,
<code>echo</code>, <code>gin</code> &#8212; which all expose <code>r.Get(path,
h)</code> style APIs
</li>
</ol>
<p>
For a project this size, the stdlib mux patterns are the right call; no
dependency needed.
</p>
<h3>
One thing to update
</h3>
<p>
Your <code>server_test.go</code> has a <code>&quot;wrong method&quot;</code>
case expecting 405. That still passes with the pattern approach, since
the mux produces the 405 itself &#8212; but the body text changes from <code>&quot;method
not allowed&quot;</code> to Go's default <code>&quot;Method Not Allowed&quot;</code>.
The test only asserts the status for that case, so it's fine as written.
</p>
<p>
Want me to apply the pattern-based refactor to <code>server.go</code>?
</p>
  </body>
</html>

#### Author
Santiago Hernandez
#### Prompt
<html>
  <head>

  </head>
  <body>
    <p style="margin-top: 0px">
      Do go mux services not automatically log requests received and print 
      them in the console
    </p>
  </body>
</html>


#### Answer **
<html>
  <head>

  </head>
  <body>
    <p style="margin-top: 0px">
      Correct &#8212; <strong>no</strong>. <code>net/http</code> and <code>ServeMux</code> 
      do <strong>zero</strong> request logging out of the box. A server can 
      handle thousands of requests and print nothing.
    </p>
    <p>
      The only thing the stdlib logs automatically is <em>errors</em>, via <code>Server.ErrorLog</code>:
    </p>
    <ul>
      <li>
        panics recovered in a handler (with stack trace)
      </li>
      <li>
        malformed requests / TLS handshake failures
      </li>
      <li>
        <code>superfluous WriteHeader call</code> warnings
      </li>
    </ul>
    <p>
      Successful requests are silent by design &#8212; the stdlib stays 
      unopinionated about log format, so you add it yourself with middleware.
    </p>
    <h3>
      Why frameworks feel different
    </h3>
    <p>
      Gin, Echo, Chi, and Fiber ship a logger middleware enabled (or one-line 
      enabled) by default, which is why you see <code>GET /foo 200 1.2ms</code> 
      in their consoles. That's the framework, not Go.
    </p>
    <h3>
      Adding it yourself
    </h3>
    <p>
      Middleware is just a function that wraps an <code>http.Handler</code>:
    </p>
    <pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="807,1726" data-copilot-content-offset="813,1723" data-copilot-code-block-index="0" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>// logging logs method, path, status, size, and duration for each request.
func logging(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		start := time.Now()
		rec := &amp;statusRecorder{ResponseWriter: w, status: http.StatusOK}

		next.ServeHTTP(rec, r)

		log.Printf(&quot;%s %s %d %dB %s %s&quot;,
			r.Method,
			r.URL.Path,
			rec.status,
			rec.bytes,
			time.Since(start).Round(time.Microsecond),
			r.RemoteAddr,
		)
	})
}

// statusRecorder captures the status code and body size, which the
// ResponseWriter interface does not expose after the fact.
type statusRecorder struct {
http.ResponseWriter
status int
bytes  int
}

func (r *statusRecorder) WriteHeader(code int) {
r.status = code
r.ResponseWriter.WriteHeader(code)
}

func (r *statusRecorder) Write(b []byte) (int, error) {
n, err := r.ResponseWriter.Write(b)
r.bytes += n
return n, err
}</code></pre>
<p>
Then wrap the mux in <code>newRouter</code>:
</p>
<pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="1763,1912" data-copilot-content-offset="1769,1909" data-copilot-code-block-index="1" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>func newRouter() http.Handler {
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.HandleFunc(&quot;GET &quot;+helloWorldPath, helloWorldHandler)
return logging(mux)
}</code></pre>
<p>
Output looks like:
</p>
<pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="1933,2016" data-copilot-content-offset="1937,2013" data-copilot-code-block-index="2"><code>2026/09/24 10:14:02 GET /api/v1/hello-world 200 13B 118.2&#181;s 127.0.0.1:53114</code></pre>
<h3>
The wrapper detail that matters
</h3>
<p>
<code>http.ResponseWriter</code> gives you no way to read back the
status code after it's written, so you <em>must</em> embed it in a
struct that intercepts <code>WriteHeader</code> and <code>Write</code>.
Note the 405 and 404 cases still get logged correctly, because the mux
writes those through the same wrapped writer.
</p>
<p>
One caveat: embedding loses optional interfaces like <code>http.Flusher</code>
and <code>http.Hijacker</code>. For SSE or WebSockets you'd add:
</p>
<pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="2461,2573" data-copilot-content-offset="2467,2570" data-copilot-code-block-index="3" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>func (r *statusRecorder) Flush() {
if f, ok := r.ResponseWriter.(http.Flusher); ok {
f.Flush()
}
}</code></pre>
<h3>
Structured logging alternative
</h3>
<p>
Go 1.21+ has <code>log/slog</code> if you'd prefer JSON:
</p>
<pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="2657,2804" data-copilot-content-offset="2663,2801" data-copilot-code-block-index="4" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>slog.Info(&quot;request&quot;,
&quot;method&quot;, r.Method,
&quot;path&quot;, r.URL.Path,
&quot;status&quot;, rec.status,
&quot;duration_ms&quot;, time.Since(start).Milliseconds(),
)</code></pre>
<p>
Want me to add the logging middleware to <code>server.go</code> (plus a
test asserting it doesn't alter the response)?
</p>
  </body>
</html>
